position: both — *an interesting book*, *the book was interesting*
takes: often *it's interesting* + *to*-infinitive or *that*-clause: *It's interesting to see how kids learn*, *It's interesting that nobody noticed*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *interesting* describes the thing that holds your attention; *interested* describes the person. *I'm interesting* praises yourself; *I'm interested* is almost always what you mean. Russian *мне интересно* is *I'm interested* or *I wonder*, never *it's interesting for me*. Said in a flat voice, *That's interesting* is often a polite way of not saying you disagree.

senses.gloss: Holding your attention because it is new, unusual or makes you want to know more.
examples: We had a really *interesting* conversation about the election.
Her new book is *more interesting* than her first one.
The *most interesting* part of the tour was the old jail.

senses.gloss: Strange or unexpected; used politely instead of saying something is odd or bad.
examples: Pineapple on a hot dog? That's an *interesting* choice.
Well, that was an *interesting* meeting — nobody agreed on anything.

position: both — *interested students*, *the students were interested*; in the sense 'personally involved' almost always before a noun: *an interested party*
takes: *in* + noun or *-ing*: *interested in history*, *interested in buying*; *to*-infinitive with verbs of learning: *interested to hear*, *interested to know*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: The preposition is *in* — not *interested about*, *for* or *by*. *I'm interested in learning Spanish* means you want to; *I'd be interested to hear what you think* means you would like to find out. *uninterested* is not interested; *disinterested* traditionally means fair, with nothing to gain, although many Americans use it for both. *I'm interesting* means you think you are fascinating — say *I'm interested*.

senses.gloss: Wanting to know or learn more about something, and giving it your attention.
examples: My son is really *interested* in dinosaurs.
I'm not *interested* in politics.
The kids seemed *more interested* in the snacks than in the movie.

senses.gloss: Wanting to do, have or take part in something.
examples: Are you *interested* in joining our team?
We already have three *interested* buyers for the house.
If you're *interested*, call me before Friday.

senses.gloss: Personally involved in a situation and likely to be affected by the result.
examples: The city will hear from all *interested* parties before it votes.
Copies of the report went to every *interested* group.

position: both — *a boring class*, *the class was boring*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *boring* is the cause, *bored* is the feeling. *I'm boring* means other people find you dull (я скучный); *I'm bored* is Russian *мне скучно*. In the same way: *The class was boring*, so *the students were bored*.

senses.gloss: Not interesting; making you feel tired and impatient.
examples: The first hour of the movie was so *boring* that I fell asleep.
He's a nice guy, but his stories are kind of *boring*.
Doing taxes is the *most boring* job of the year.

position: both — *bored kids*, *the kids were bored*
takes: *with* + noun or *-ing*: *bored with my job*; *by* + noun: *bored by the lecture*; *bored of* is common in casual speech, but many teachers mark it wrong
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *I'm bored* (мне скучно) is about how you feel; *I'm boring* (я скучный) is about how others see you. *bored with* something that has gone on too long is closer to Russian *надоело*: *I'm bored with my job*. Common intensifiers: *bored to death*, *bored to tears*, *bored stiff*.

senses.gloss: Tired and impatient because you have nothing interesting to do.
examples: The kids get *bored* on long car trips.
A *bored* teenager is often a teenager looking for trouble.
Nobody at that meeting looked *more bored* than the boss.

senses.gloss: Tired of something because it has gone on too long or never changes.
examples: She was *bored* with her job and started looking for a new one.
After ten years in the same town, he was *bored* with small-town life.

position: both — *an exciting game*, *the game was exciting*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *exciting* is about the thing, *excited* about the person: *an exciting game*, *excited fans*. It is always positive, never Russian *волнующий* in the sense of worrying: for *я волнуюсь перед экзаменом* say *I'm nervous about the exam*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel eager, happy and full of energy.
examples: Moving to New York was the *most exciting* thing I've ever done.
It was an *exciting* game right up to the last second.
We have some *exciting* news — we're having a baby!

position: both — *excited fans*, *the fans were excited*; the physics sense mostly before a noun: *an excited atom*
takes: *about* + noun or *-ing*: *excited about the trip*; *to*-infinitive: *excited to see you*; *that*-clause; *for* + person or event, especially in American speech: *I'm so excited for you*, *excited for the weekend*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *I'm excited* is Russian *я жду не дождусь*, *я в предвкушении* or *я так рад*, not *возбуждённый*, which in Russian often sounds agitated or sexual. *I'm exciting* is wrong. *Don't get excited* can mean *calm down*, and *Don't get too excited* means don't expect too much. You are *excited about* a thing and *excited for* a person who has good news.

senses.gloss: Very happy and eager about something that is happening or will happen.
examples: The kids are so *excited* about Christmas.
I'm really *excited* to start my new job.
I've never seen him *more excited* than the day he got his first car.

senses.gloss: Nervous, upset or unable to stay calm.
examples: Calm down — there's no need to get *excited*.
The dog gets *excited* and barks whenever someone knocks.

senses.gloss: Sexually aroused.
examples: The study measured heart rate when subjects were sexually *excited*.
Doctors say it can take longer for older adults to become sexually *excited*.

senses.gloss: In physics, having more energy than the normal, lowest state.
examples: An *excited* electron gives off light as it drops to a lower energy level.
The laser works by pumping atoms into an *excited* state.

position: both — *a surprising result*, *the result was surprising*
takes: often *it's surprising* + *that*-clause or *how*-clause: *It's surprising that she said no*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *surprising* only means unexpected, good or bad. Russian *удивительный* in the sense of wonderful is *amazing*: *an amazing view* (удивительный вид), not *a surprising view*. *It's not surprising* and *hardly surprising* are the usual ways to say *неудивительно*. The person is *surprised*.

senses.gloss: Unexpected, and so causing surprise.
examples: The results of the survey were *surprising*.
It's *surprising* how many people still don't wear seat belts.
The *most surprising* thing about the trip was how cheap it was.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *I was surprised*; before a noun mainly with look, face, expression: *a surprised look*
takes: *at* or *by* + noun: *surprised at the price*, *surprised by the news*; *to*-infinitive: *surprised to see you*; *that*-clause; *at* + person, disapproving: *I'm surprised at you*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: The person is *surprised*, the cause is *surprising*: *I was surprised*; *The news was surprising*. Not *surprised of*. *I wouldn't be surprised if* is Russian *не удивлюсь, если*. *I'm surprised at you* is not neutral — like *ты меня удивляешь*, it scolds someone for behaving worse than you expected: *Cheating on a test? I'm surprised at you*.

senses.gloss: Feeling surprise because something happened that you did not expect.
examples: I was *surprised* to see her at the party.
Nobody was *more surprised* by the win than the coach.
She gave me a *surprised* look.

position: both — *confusing instructions*, *the instructions were confusing*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *confusing* is what makes you lose track; *confused* is how you feel: *The instructions were confusing, and I was confused*. *I'm confusing* means you confuse other people.

senses.gloss: Difficult to understand; not clear.
examples: The tax forms are really *confusing*.
The ending of the movie was *more confusing* than the rest of it.
It's *confusing* when two people on the team have the same name.

position: both — *a confused student*, *the student was confused*
takes: *about* + noun or *wh*-clause: *confused about the rules*, *confused about what to do*; *by* + the cause: *confused by the signs*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: False friend: *confused* is *растерянный* or *сбитый с толку*, not *сконфуженный* — that is *embarrassed*. The person is *confused*; the cause is *confusing*. *confused with* is usually the verb: *He is often confused with his brother* (его путают с братом).

senses.gloss: Unable to understand something or to decide what to do.
examples: I'm *confused* — which bus do I take?
Students were *confused* about the new schedule.
I was even *more confused* after he explained it.

senses.gloss: Unable to think clearly or know where you are, because of illness, age or an injury.
examples: After the fall, the patient was *confused* and couldn't remember his address.
Call a doctor if an older person suddenly seems *confused*.

senses.gloss: Mixed up and not clear or orderly.
examples: The witness gave a *confused* account of the accident.
The message from the campaign was *confused* and contradictory.

position: both — *a tiring day*, *the day was tiring*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *tiring* wears out your body; *tiresome* is boring or annoying: *a tiring hike*, *a tiresome neighbor*. *I'm tiring* is the verb and means *I'm getting tired*; for *я устал* say *I'm tired*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel tired.
examples: It was a long, *tiring* day at work.
Driving at night is *more tiring* than driving during the day.
Taking care of twins is *tiring*.

position: both — *tired kids*, *the kids were tired*; *tired of* only after a verb
takes: *of* + noun or *-ing* — fed up: *tired of waiting*; *from* + noun or *-ing* — the physical cause: *tired from the trip*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: Russian *устал от* splits in English: *I'm tired from work* (устал после работы) but *I'm tired of work* (работа надоела). *sick and tired of* is a strong *надоело*. The person is *tired*; the cause is *tiring*.

senses.gloss: Needing rest or sleep.
examples: I'm too *tired* to cook tonight.
She came home *tired* from a twelve-hour shift.
You look *more tired* than usual — are you OK?

senses.gloss: No longer interested in or patient with something because it has gone on too long.
examples: I'm *tired* of hearing the same excuses.
People are getting *tired* of all the political ads.

senses.gloss: Used too often or too long, and so no longer fresh or interesting.
examples: He told the same *tired* old jokes at every party.
The hotel lobby looked a little *tired*, with worn carpet and faded chairs.

position: both — *a terrifying moment*, *the moment was terrifying*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: A strong word: *absolutely* or *really terrifying* sounds more natural than *very terrifying*. Do not confuse it with *terrific*, which means *great*: *You did a terrific job* (отличная работа). The thing is *terrifying*; the person is *terrified*.

senses.gloss: So frightening that it fills you with fear.
examples: Being stuck in the elevator was *terrifying*.
It was the *most terrifying* movie I've ever seen.
There was one *terrifying* moment when the plane suddenly dropped.

position: both — *a terrified child*, *the child was terrified*
takes: *of* + noun or *-ing*: *terrified of spiders*; *to*-infinitive: *terrified to go outside*; *that*-clause
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: A strong word: *absolutely* or *completely terrified* sounds more natural than *very terrified*. Not *terrified from*. The person is *terrified*; the thing is *terrifying*.

senses.gloss: Extremely frightened.
examples: My little sister is *terrified* of dogs.
The *terrified* passengers screamed as the bus slid on the ice.
I was *terrified* that I would fail the exam.

position: both — *an amazing view*, *the view was amazing*
takes: often *it's amazing* + *that*-clause or *how*-clause: *It's amazing how fast kids grow*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: In everyday American speech *amazing* mostly just means *great* — *The food was amazing* — and it is used so often it can sound empty. A strong word: *absolutely* or *really amazing*, rather than *very amazing*. Russian *удивительный* meaning simply unexpected is *surprising*. The person is *amazed*.

senses.gloss: Extremely good; wonderful.
examples: We had an *amazing* time in Hawaii.
Your mom's lasagna is *amazing*.
That was the *most amazing* concert I've ever been to.

senses.gloss: So unusual or unexpected that it causes great surprise.
examples: It's *amazing* how fast kids pick up languages.
It's *amazing* that nobody was hurt in the crash.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *I was amazed*; before a noun mainly with look, face, crowd: *an amazed look*
takes: *at* or *by* + noun: *amazed at the view*, *amazed by her talent*; *to*-infinitive: *amazed to find*; *that*-clause; *how*-clause
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *amazed* is stronger than *surprised* and usually pleasant. Not *amazed of*. The person is *amazed*; *I'm amazing* is bragging.

senses.gloss: Very surprised, often in a pleasant way.
examples: I was *amazed* at how much the city had changed.
We were *amazed* to find the store still open at midnight.
The *amazed* crowd watched the rocket climb into the sky.

position: both — *disappointing results*, *the results were disappointing*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: Russian often says *не оправдал ожиданий*; English simply uses the adjective: *The results were disappointing*. Spelling: one *s*, two *p*s. The thing is *disappointing*; the person is *disappointed*.

senses.gloss: Not as good as you hoped or expected.
examples: The movie got great reviews, but I found it *disappointing*.
Sales this quarter were *more disappointing* than expected.
It's *disappointing* that the park is closed again.

position: both — *disappointed fans*, *the fans were disappointed*
takes: *in* + person: *disappointed in you*; *with* or *by* + thing: *disappointed with the service*; *about* + event: *disappointed about the loss*; *to*-infinitive: *disappointed to hear*; *that*-clause
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *disappointed in* someone is personal and it hurts: *I'm disappointed in you* (ты меня разочаровал). For a result or a service use *with* or *by*. Not *disappointed of*. *I'm disappointing* means you let others down — say *I'm disappointed*.

senses.gloss: Unhappy because something was not as good as you hoped or did not happen.
examples: I was *disappointed* with the hotel.
The coach said he was *disappointed* in the team's effort.
Thousands of *disappointed* fans left before the game ended.

position: both — *a relaxing bath*, *the bath was relaxing*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *relaxing* is the thing that calms you: *a relaxing vacation*. *relaxed* is usually the person, but it can also describe a place or style: *a relaxed atmosphere* (непринуждённая атмосфера). *I'm relaxing* is the verb — *я отдыхаю*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel calm and rested.
examples: We spent a *relaxing* week at the lake.
A hot shower is *relaxing* after a long day.
Fishing is *more relaxing* than you might think.

position: both — *a relaxed atmosphere*, *she seemed relaxed*
takes: *about* + noun or *-ing*: *relaxed about the deadline*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: Unlike most *-ed* adjectives, *relaxed* describes places, events and rules as well as people: *a relaxed restaurant* (непринуждённый), *relaxed rules* (нестрогие). What makes you calm is *relaxing*. *I'm relaxed* is how you feel; *I'm relaxing* is what you are doing.

senses.gloss: Calm and not worried or tense.
examples: You seem much *more relaxed* since you changed jobs.
She was *relaxed* and smiling during the interview.
Keep your shoulders *relaxed* while you type.

senses.gloss: Informal and comfortable, not stiff.
examples: The restaurant has a *relaxed* atmosphere and a great patio.
The dress code at the office is pretty *relaxed*.

senses.gloss: Not strict or firmly controlled.
examples: Some schools have a *relaxed* attitude toward phones in class.
Under the *relaxed* guidelines, restaurants could seat more people.

position: both — *an embarrassing mistake*, *the mistake was embarrassing*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: Spelling: two *r*s and two *s*s. The thing is *embarrassing*; the person is *embarrassed*. *It's embarrassing* (неловко, стыдно) is about looking foolish, not about guilt — for moral shame English uses *shameful*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel awkward, silly or ashamed in front of other people.
examples: It was so *embarrassing* when I called my teacher 'Mom.'
My dad tells the *most embarrassing* stories about me.
Forgetting his name was really *embarrassing*.

senses.gloss: Causing problems for someone's public image or position.
examples: The leaked emails were *embarrassing* for the senator.
The mistake was politically *embarrassing* for the mayor.

position: both — *an embarrassed laugh*, *he was embarrassed*
takes: *about* or *by* + noun or *-ing*: *embarrassed about my accent*; *to*-infinitive: *embarrassed to ask*; *that*-clause; *for* + person — awkward on someone else's behalf: *I was embarrassed for him*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: False friend: *сконфуженный* is *embarrassed*, not *confused*. *embarrassed* (неловко, стыдно) is about looking foolish; *ashamed* is about having done something wrong. *embarrassed for* someone is what Russian calls *испанский стыд*. Spelling: two *r*s, two *s*s.

senses.gloss: Feeling awkward, shy or ashamed because of how you look to other people.
examples: I was too *embarrassed* to tell anyone.
He gave an *embarrassed* laugh and turned red.
I've never been *more embarrassed* in my life.

senses.gloss: Short of money; used formally or humorously in *financially embarrassed*.
examples: The company was financially *embarrassed* and couldn't pay its suppliers.
I'm a little financially *embarrassed* until payday.

position: both — *a satisfying job*, *the job was satisfying*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: Do not mix up *satisfying* (it feels good) with *satisfactory* (удовлетворительный — only good enough): *a satisfying meal* is a good one; *a satisfactory grade* is just OK. The person is *satisfied*.

senses.gloss: Giving you pleasure because it is what you wanted, or because you did it well.
examples: Teaching is hard but very *satisfying* work.
There's nothing *more satisfying* than finishing a big project.
It was *satisfying* to finally beat them.

senses.gloss: Of food, filling enough that you are no longer hungry.
examples: Oatmeal makes a cheap, *satisfying* breakfast.
The soup was hot and *satisfying*.

senses.gloss: Of an answer or explanation, good enough to accept.
examples: Nobody could give me a *satisfying* answer.
Scientists still don't have a *satisfying* explanation for why we dream.

position: both — *satisfied customers*, *the customers were satisfied*
takes: *with* + noun: *satisfied with the result*; *that*-clause — convinced: *satisfied that he was telling the truth*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: Say *satisfied with* when you mean happy with something — not *satisfied of*. *self-satisfied* is too pleased with yourself. The opposite is *dissatisfied*; *unsatisfied* means a need is still not met: *unsatisfied demand*. The cause is *satisfying*.

senses.gloss: Pleased because you got what you wanted or something was done well.
examples: Are you *satisfied* with your new car?
We want every customer to leave *satisfied*.
Our *most satisfied* customers are the ones who come back.

senses.gloss: Sure that something is true, especially after checking.
examples: The police were *satisfied* that the fire was an accident.
I'm *satisfied* the numbers are correct.

position: both — *an annoying noise*, *the noise was annoying*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *He's so annoying* (он такой надоедливый, бесит) is about the person who causes it; *I'm annoyed* (я раздражён) is how you feel. *I'm annoying* says that you bother people.

senses.gloss: Making you a little angry or impatient.
examples: That car alarm is really *annoying*.
My little brother is the *most annoying* person in the world.
It's *annoying* when people talk during a movie.

position: both — *an annoyed customer*, *the customer was annoyed*
takes: *with* or *at* + person: *annoyed with me*; *at* or *about* + thing: *annoyed about the delay*; *that*-clause; *to*-infinitive: *annoyed to find*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *annoyed* is milder than *angry*. The person is *annoyed*; the cause is *annoying*: *I'm annoyed* (я раздражён, меня это злит), *It's annoying* (это раздражает).

senses.gloss: Slightly angry or impatient.
examples: She was *annoyed* with me for being late.
I get *annoyed* when people don't return my calls.
The *annoyed* driver behind us kept honking.

position: both — *shocking news*, *the news was shocking*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: British English also uses *shocking* for simply very bad (*shocking weather*); Americans say *terrible* or *awful*. The thing is *shocking*; the person is *shocked*.

senses.gloss: Very surprising and upsetting.
examples: The news of his death was *shocking*.
The report reveals some *shocking* numbers about child poverty.
The *most shocking* part was that nobody called the police.

senses.gloss: Morally wrong or offensive.
examples: The way they treated those workers was *shocking*.
The judge called it a *shocking* abuse of power.

position: both — *shocked neighbors*, *the neighbors were shocked*
takes: *at* or *by* + noun: *shocked at the price*, *shocked by the news*; *to*-infinitive: *shocked to learn*; *that*-clause
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *shocked* is the feeling; the medical condition is *in shock*: *She was in shock after the crash* (в шоковом состоянии). In American speech *I got shocked* usually means an electric shock — that is the verb. The cause is *shocking*.

senses.gloss: Very surprised and upset by something unexpected.
examples: We were *shocked* to hear about the accident.
Neighbors said they were *shocked* by the arrest.
I've never seen him look *more shocked*.

senses.gloss: Offended because something seems morally wrong or rude.
examples: Some viewers were *shocked* by the language in the show.
She pretended to be *shocked*, but she was laughing.

position: both — *a frightening experience*, *the experience was frightening*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: Russian *страшно* is two things in English: *It's frightening* (это страшно) and *I'm frightened* or *I'm scared* (мне страшно). In everyday American speech *scary* is more common: *a scary movie*. The person is *frightened*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel afraid.
examples: Hearing footsteps behind you at night is *frightening*.
Prices are rising at a *frightening* rate.
It was *more frightening* than any horror movie.

position: both — *a frightened child*, *the child was frightened*
takes: *of* + noun or *-ing*: *frightened of the dark*; *by* + a particular event: *frightened by the noise*; *to*-infinitive: *frightened to go out*; *that*-clause
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *frightened of* is a general fear (боится темноты); *frightened by* is a reaction to one event (испугался шума). In speech Americans usually say *scared*. Unlike *afraid*, *frightened* goes before a noun: *a frightened animal*, never *an afraid animal*.

senses.gloss: Feeling fear; afraid.
examples: The *frightened* cat hid under the bed.
She's *frightened* of flying.
I was *more frightened* than I let the kids see.

position: both — *a worrying trend*, *the trend is worrying*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: As an adjective *worrying* is more British. Americans more often say *worrisome*, *troubling* or, in news and business, *concerning*: *a worrisome trend*. *Stop worrying* is the verb (перестань волноваться), not the adjective. The person is *worried*.

senses.gloss: Making you anxious that something bad may happen.
examples: Doctors say the rise in cases is *worrying*.
There's been a *worrying* drop in reading scores.
The *most worrying* thing is that nobody knows where he is.

position: both — *worried parents*, *the parents were worried*
takes: *about* + noun or *-ing*: *worried about money*; *that*-clause: *worried that he'd get lost*; *for* + person or their safety: *worried for her*; *by* + a particular cause: *worried by the news*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *I'm worried* is a feeling now (я волнуюсь, беспокоюсь); *I worry* is a habit (я вечно переживаю). To comfort someone, the usual phrase is *Don't worry*. Not *worried of*. The cause is *worrying*, or in American English more often *worrisome*.

senses.gloss: Anxious because you think something bad has happened or may happen.
examples: My mom gets *worried* if I don't call.
I'm *more worried* about the test than I was last week.
The doctor had a *worried* look on her face.

position: both — *an exhausting trip*, *the trip was exhausting*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: False friend: *исчерпывающий* is *exhaustive* (*an exhaustive list*), not *exhausting*. *exhausting* is what wears you out; the person is *exhausted*.

senses.gloss: Making you extremely tired.
examples: Moving across the country was *exhausting*.
The *most exhausting* part of the job is the commute.
After an *exhausting* week, we slept until noon.

position: both — *exhausted firefighters*, *the firefighters were exhausted*
takes: *from* + noun or *-ing*: *exhausted from the trip*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: A strong word: *completely* or *absolutely exhausted* sounds more natural than *very exhausted*. It is much stronger than *tired* — not just *устал*, but *вымотан*. *exhausted* supplies are used up (исчерпаны); *exhaustive* means complete (исчерпывающий).

senses.gloss: Extremely tired.
examples: I was completely *exhausted* after the race.
The *exhausted* firefighters finally got some sleep.
She looked even *more exhausted* than the day before.

senses.gloss: Completely used up, with nothing left.
examples: The land was dry and *exhausted* after years of growing cotton.
Crews sealed the *exhausted* mine in the 1950s.

position: both — *a fascinating story*, *the story was fascinating*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *fascinating* is much stronger than *interesting*, so it goes more naturally with *absolutely* or *really* than with *very*. The person is *fascinated*.

senses.gloss: Extremely interesting.
examples: The museum has a *fascinating* exhibit on ancient Egypt.
I find his ideas absolutely *fascinating*.
It was the *most fascinating* class I took in college.

position: both — *fascinated kids*, *the kids were fascinated*
takes: *by* or *with* + noun: *fascinated by insects*, *fascinated with old maps*; *to*-infinitive: *fascinated to learn*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *interested in*, but *fascinated by* or *with* — not *fascinated in*. *fascinated* is much stronger than *interested*. The thing is *fascinating*.

senses.gloss: Extremely interested, and unable to stop watching or thinking about something.
examples: The kids were *fascinated* by the sharks.
He's always been *fascinated* with old maps.
She was *fascinated* to learn that her family came from Ireland.

position: both — *depressing news*, *the news was depressing*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *depressing* is the thing that makes you sad (угнетающий, тоскливый); the person is *depressed*. Russian *депрессивный* covers both, so *депрессивный фильм* is *a depressing movie*, never *a depressed movie*. *I'm depressing* means you make other people sad.

senses.gloss: Making you feel sad and without hope.
examples: The news is so *depressing* these days.
Winter here is long, gray and *depressing*.
It's the *most depressing* movie I've ever seen.

position: both — *a depressed teenager*, *she seemed depressed*; the economic sense is common before a noun: *a depressed area*
takes: *about* + noun or *-ing*: *depressed about losing the job*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: In everyday speech *depressed* can just mean *very sad*, but it is also the medical word for clinical depression, so use it with care. *a depressed area* is not sad but poor, with few jobs. The cause is *depressing*.

senses.gloss: Very sad and without hope, especially for a long time.
examples: He's been *depressed* since his dog died.
I get kind of *depressed* when it rains all week.
She felt *more depressed* than ever after the holidays.

senses.gloss: Suffering from depression as a medical condition.
examples: Clinically *depressed* patients often have trouble sleeping.
Talk to a doctor if you think you might be *depressed*.

senses.gloss: Having little business activity, few jobs or lower prices than usual.
examples: The factory closing left the town economically *depressed*.
Home prices are still *depressed* in parts of the Midwest.

position: both — *a frustrating problem*, *the problem was frustrating*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: Russian has no single word: *frustrating* is what makes you feel *досадно*, *бесит* or *руки опускаются* because you can't get something done. It is an everyday word, not the psychology term *фрустрирующий*. The person is *frustrated*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel annoyed and discouraged because you cannot do or get what you want.
examples: It's *frustrating* when the website keeps crashing.
Losing in the last minute was the *most frustrating* part.
Learning to drive a stick shift can be really *frustrating*.

position: both — *frustrated voters*, *the voters were frustrated*; in the sense 'never became what they wanted' only before a noun: *a frustrated writer*
takes: *with* or *by* + noun: *frustrated with the software*, *frustrated by the delays*; *at* + thing: *frustrated at the lack of progress*; *that*-clause
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *frustrated* is an everyday word (раздосадован, злюсь, что не получается), not a psychology term like *фрустрированный*. It is not *upset* (расстроен) or *disappointed*: *frustrated* means you keep trying and it still doesn't work. Before a noun it can mean someone who never became what they wanted: *a frustrated actor*.

senses.gloss: Annoyed and discouraged because you cannot do or get what you want.
examples: I get so *frustrated* when my computer freezes.
Voters are *frustrated* with both parties.
The longer we waited, the *more frustrated* we got.

senses.gloss: Wanting to be a particular kind of person, such as an artist, but never having managed it.
examples: He's a *frustrated* actor who ended up selling insurance.
Every *frustrated* novelist in the office wanted to write the newsletter.

position: both — *an amusing story*, *the story was amusing*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *amusing* is milder than *funny* — it makes you smile rather than laugh out loud. The person is *amused*.

senses.gloss: Funny and entertaining in a way that makes you smile.
examples: He told an *amusing* story about his first day at work.
I didn't find his jokes very *amusing*.
Her speech was *more amusing* than I expected.

position: both — *an amused smile*, *she looked amused*
takes: *by* or *at* + noun: *amused by the puppy*; *to*-infinitive: *amused to see*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *not amused* is a polite way to say someone was annoyed: *The boss was not amused* (шефу было не до смеха). *keep someone amused* means keep them busy and entertained. The cause is *amusing*.

senses.gloss: Finding something funny.
examples: She seemed *amused* by my accent.
He watched us with an *amused* smile.
My teacher was not *amused* when I fell asleep in class.

senses.gloss: Busy and entertained, so that you are not bored.
examples: Coloring books kept the kids *amused* on the flight.
There's plenty in the city to keep you *amused*.

position: both — *an astonishing comeback*, *the comeback was astonishing*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: Stronger and more formal than *surprising*. Close to *amazing*, but it never just means *great* the way *amazing* does in speech. The person is *astonished*.

senses.gloss: So surprising that it is hard to believe.
examples: The team made an *astonishing* comeback in the fourth quarter.
It's *astonishing* how little the town has changed.
The *most astonishing* thing is that he survived.

position: both — *an astonished expression*, *we were astonished*
takes: *at* or *by* + noun: *astonished at the news*; *to*-infinitive: *astonished to find*; *that*-clause
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: Stronger than *surprised* and a little formal. Not *astonished of*. The cause is *astonishing*.

senses.gloss: Extremely surprised.
examples: I was *astonished* to see how big the kids had gotten.
Doctors were *astonished* by her recovery.
He stared at me with an *astonished* expression.

position: both — *a pleasing design*, *the design is pleasing*
takes: *to* + person or sense: *pleasing to the eye*, *pleasing to customers*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *pleasing* is formal and usually describes how something looks or sounds: *a pleasing color*. In conversation Americans say *nice* or *pleasant*. The person who feels the pleasure is *pleased*.

senses.gloss: Giving pleasure or satisfaction; attractive.
examples: The colors are *pleasing* to the eye.
The new park is a *pleasing* addition to downtown.
The second design was *more pleasing* than the first.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *I was pleased*; before a noun mainly with smile, look, expression: *a pleased smile*
takes: *with* + noun: *pleased with the results*; *about* + noun; *for* + person: *pleased for you*; *to*-infinitive: *pleased to meet you*; *that*-clause
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *pleased with* something is being satisfied with it (доволен); *pleased for* someone is being happy about their good news (рад за тебя). *pleased with yourself* often means too proud of yourself. *Pleased to meet you* is correct but formal; Americans usually say *Nice to meet you*.

senses.gloss: Happy and satisfied with something.
examples: The coach was *pleased* with how the team played.
She looked very *pleased* with herself.
I've never been *more pleased* with a haircut.

senses.gloss: Glad to do or hear something; used especially in polite phrases.
examples: We are *pleased* to announce the opening of our new store.
I'm *pleased* that you could come.

position: both — *a thrilling finish*, *the finish was thrilling*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *thrilling* is stronger than *exciting* and usually describes events: *a thrilling finish*. The person is *thrilled*. A *thriller* is the noun for a suspense book or movie.

senses.gloss: Extremely exciting.
examples: The game had a *thrilling* finish.
Riding a roller coaster for the first time was *thrilling*.
It was the *most thrilling* race of the season.

position: predicative only — *I'm thrilled*, *she was thrilled*; not normally before a noun
takes: *with* or *about* + noun: *thrilled with the gift*; *to*-infinitive: *thrilled to be here*; *that*-clause; *for* + person: *thrilled for you*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: Very strong — Russian *в восторге*, *безумно рад*. *not thrilled* is understatement for unhappy: *She wasn't thrilled about the idea* (ей идея не понравилась). The cause is *thrilling*.

senses.gloss: Extremely happy and excited.
examples: We're *thrilled* to have you here.
My parents were *thrilled* with the news.
I wasn't exactly *thrilled* about working on Sunday.

position: both — *overwhelming support*, *the job felt overwhelming*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *an overwhelming majority* is *подавляющее большинство*, but Russian *подавляющий* fits only that sense; for feelings and workload use *ошеломляющий* or *непосильный*. The person who can't cope is *overwhelmed*.

senses.gloss: Very great in amount or strength, so that nothing can compete with it.
examples: The bill passed with *overwhelming* support.
The evidence against him was *overwhelming*.
An *overwhelming* majority of voters said yes.

senses.gloss: So strong or so much that it is hard to deal with.
examples: The first week at a new job can be *overwhelming*.
She felt an *overwhelming* urge to cry.
College applications are *more overwhelming* than most parents remember.

position: both — *overwhelmed nurses*, *the nurses were overwhelmed*
takes: *by* or *with* + noun: *overwhelmed with work*, *overwhelmed by grief*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *overwhelmed* is not only negative: *overwhelmed with gratitude* (переполнен благодарностью) is a good feeling. For *я не справляюсь* say *I'm overwhelmed*, not *I'm overwhelming*.

senses.gloss: Having too much to do or deal with, so that you cannot cope.
examples: Nurses are *overwhelmed* with patients this winter.
I feel totally *overwhelmed* right now.
The *overwhelmed* staff couldn't answer every call.

senses.gloss: Deeply affected by a strong emotion.
examples: She was *overwhelmed* with joy when she saw her son.
We were *overwhelmed* by the kindness of strangers.

position: both — *an alarming rate*, *the numbers are alarming*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *alarming* is what makes you worried (тревожный): *at an alarming rate*. The person is *alarmed*.

senses.gloss: Causing worry or fear that something bad is happening.
examples: Glaciers are melting at an *alarming* rate.
The number of cases is *alarming*.
The *most alarming* part of the report was about drinking water.

position: both — *an alarmed look*, *they were alarmed*; in the sense 'fitted with an alarm' mostly after a verb: *the door is alarmed*
takes: *at* or *by* + noun: *alarmed at the news*; *to*-infinitive: *alarmed to find*; *that*-clause
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *alarmed* is worried, not panicked — Russian *встревожен*. On a sign, *This door is alarmed* means it has an alarm, not that the door is scared. The cause is *alarming*.

senses.gloss: Worried or frightened that something dangerous or bad might happen.
examples: Parents are *alarmed* by the rise in vaping.
Don't be *alarmed* — it's only a fire drill.
Neighbors grew *more alarmed* as the smoke got thicker.

senses.gloss: Fitted with an alarm that goes off if it is opened.
examples: Emergency exit only — door is *alarmed*.
All the windows on the ground floor are *alarmed*.

position: both — *a puzzling question*, *the question was puzzling*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: The cause is *puzzling* (непонятный, загадочный); the person is *puzzled* (озадачен). *puzzling* is about something you can't explain; *confusing* is about something badly organized or unclear.

senses.gloss: Hard to understand or explain.
examples: His sudden decision to quit is *puzzling*.
There's something *puzzling* about the timeline.
The *most puzzling* thing is why nobody noticed.

position: both — *a puzzled look*, *she looked puzzled*
takes: *by* + noun: *puzzled by his answer*; *about* or *as to* + noun or *wh*-clause: *puzzled about why she left*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *puzzled* means you are thinking hard about something you can't explain; *confused* means you have lost track. The cause is *puzzling*.

senses.gloss: Confused because you cannot understand or explain something.
examples: He gave me a *puzzled* look.
Scientists are *puzzled* by the strange signals.
I'm still *puzzled* about why she left so early.

position: both — *an irritating habit*, *the habit is irritating*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *irritating* is close to *annoying*, often about something that keeps happening. The person is *irritated*. Like Russian *раздражающий*, it also describes what makes skin or eyes sore.

senses.gloss: Annoying, especially because it keeps happening.
examples: He has an *irritating* habit of cracking his knuckles.
The *most irritating* thing about the app is the pop-up ads.
That buzzing noise is so *irritating*.

senses.gloss: Making skin, eyes or another part of the body sore or red.
examples: Some soaps are *irritating* to sensitive skin.
Smoke can be *irritating* to the eyes and throat.

position: both — *an irritated voice*, *she sounded irritated*
takes: *with* + person: *irritated with him*; *at* or *by* + thing: *irritated by the noise*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *irritated* is about as strong as *annoyed* and weaker than *angry*. The cause is *irritating*. For skin and eyes, *irritated* means sore or red, not angry.

senses.gloss: Annoyed and impatient.
examples: She sounded *irritated* on the phone.
I get *irritated* when people cut in line.
He was *more irritated* by the delay than by the price.

senses.gloss: Of skin or eyes, sore, red or itchy.
examples: My eyes get *irritated* from the chlorine.
Use a gentle cream on *irritated* skin.

position: both — *a disgusting smell*, *the smell was disgusting*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: A strong word: *absolutely* or *really disgusting*. Russian *отвратительный* is often used for bad weather or bad service; *disgusting* is stronger and suggests something makes you feel sick. The person is *disgusted*.

senses.gloss: Extremely unpleasant to smell, taste, look at or touch.
examples: The bathroom at the gas station was *disgusting*.
This coffee tastes *disgusting*.
That's the *most disgusting* thing I've ever eaten.

senses.gloss: Morally shocking and unacceptable.
examples: What they did to those animals is *disgusting*.
It's *disgusting* that the executives got bonuses while workers lost their jobs.

position: both — *a disgusted look*, *I was disgusted*
takes: *with* + person or yourself: *disgusted with himself*; *by* or *at* + thing: *disgusted by the smell*, *disgusted at the waste*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: The person is *disgusted*; the thing is *disgusting* — *I'm disgusting* insults yourself. *disgusted* covers both physical revulsion (испытываю отвращение) and moral anger (возмущён).

senses.gloss: Feeling strong dislike or disapproval because something is unpleasant or wrong.
examples: I was *disgusted* by the smell in the fridge.
Many voters are *disgusted* with the whole campaign.
She walked out with a *disgusted* look on her face.

position: both — *encouraging news*, *the news is encouraging*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *encouraging* news gives hope (обнадёживающий); an *encouraging* person gives support (ободряющий). The person who feels hopeful is *encouraged*.

senses.gloss: Giving you hope that something will go well.
examples: The early test results are very *encouraging*.
Sales this month were *more encouraging* than last month.
It's *encouraging* to see so many young people vote.

senses.gloss: Giving someone support, praise or confidence.
examples: My coach was always *encouraging*.
She gave me an *encouraging* smile.

position: predicative only — after *be*, *feel* or *seem*: *We felt encouraged*
takes: *by* + noun: *encouraged by the results*; *to*-infinitive: *encouraged to see*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: *be encouraged to do something* is usually the verb in the passive: *Students are encouraged to ask questions* (студентам предлагают задавать вопросы) — nobody is feeling hopeful. The adjective is a feeling: *I'm encouraged by the news* (меня это обнадёживает). The cause is *encouraging*.

senses.gloss: Feeling more hopeful or confident.
examples: We're *encouraged* by the progress so far.
After the meeting, I felt *more encouraged* about the project.
Doctors were *encouraged* to see her walking again.

position: both — *an inspiring speech*, *the speech was inspiring*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *inspiring* is what makes you want to act (вдохновляющий). *inspired* can describe the person, but before a noun it usually means *brilliant*: *an inspired idea*, not *an idea that inspires*. *uninspiring* means dull.

senses.gloss: Making people want to do something good, creative or brave.
examples: Her speech at graduation was really *inspiring*.
He's one of the *most inspiring* teachers I've had.
It's an *inspiring* story of a family that never gave up.

position: both — *I feel inspired*; before a noun it usually means very good: *an inspired choice*
takes: *by* + noun: *inspired by her story*; *to*-infinitive: *inspired to write*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: The meaning changes with position: *She felt inspired* (вдохновлённая) is about the person, but *an inspired choice* or *an inspired performance* means brilliant (блестящий, удачный). *inspired by* + a source after a noun is often the verb: *a movie inspired by true events* (по мотивам реальных событий). The thing that inspires is *inspiring*.

senses.gloss: Feeling eager and excited to do something, especially something creative.
examples: After the trip, I felt *inspired* to start painting again.
Kids come out of the science museum totally *inspired*.
I've never felt *more inspired* than I did that summer.

senses.gloss: Extremely good or clever, as if done with special talent.
examples: Hiring her was an *inspired* choice.
The band gave an *inspired* performance.

senses.gloss: Influenced by a particular style, place or idea; usually joined to another word with a hyphen.
examples: The restaurant serves *Mexican-inspired* dishes.
Police believe the attack was politically *inspired*.

position: both — *a touching moment*, *the moment was touching*
form: -ing — what causes the feeling
contrast: *touching* (трогательный) is not *touchy* (обидчивый): *a touching letter*, but *a touchy subject*. The person who feels it is *touched*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel sympathy, sadness or tenderness.
examples: It was a *touching* moment when the soldier hugged his daughter.
His letter to his grandmother was very *touching*.
It's one of the *most touching* movies I've seen.

position: predicative only — *I was touched*, *she seemed touched*; not before a noun
takes: *by* + noun: *touched by your kindness*; *that*-clause: *touched that you remembered*; *to*-infinitive: *touched to receive*
form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
contrast: Like Russian *тронутый*, it can mean emotionally moved or, in old-fashioned speech, a little crazy; context makes it clear. It goes only after a verb: *I was really touched*. The thing that moves you is *touching*.

senses.gloss: Feeling grateful and emotional because someone was kind.
examples: I was really *touched* that you remembered my birthday.
She was *touched* by all the cards from her students.
I've never been *more touched* by a gift.

senses.gloss: Old-fashioned and informal: slightly crazy.
examples: Folks in town thought the old man was a little *touched*.
You'd have to be *touched* in the head to go out in this storm.
